newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia suspends 36 teachers pending abuse inquiry.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia suspends 36 teachers pending abuse inquiry.

text.p: Thirty-six Australian school teachers were stood down on Thursday while allegations of sexual abuse or misconduct against them were investigated, the New South Wales state government said.
The decision to remove the 36 teachers comes after a further 106 teachers were identified by an inquiry as posing a possible risk of sex abuse to children under their care.
"I have told the director general of school education that I don't want any chances to be taken when it comes to the safety of children," said New South Wales state premier Bob Carr.
"My absolute priority is to ensure that there is no threat to children in school," Carr said in a statement announcing the 36 stand-downs.
Carr said he had appointed a former senior judge, John Slattery, to head an inquiry into the backgrounds of the 36 teachers and the possible risks they posed to students.
Slattery will also determine which of the 106 other teachers pose an "unacceptable" risk to children and those teachers will also be removed from schools, Carr said.

A senior education department official on Wednesday told a state inquiry examining paedophilia that 106 teachers who had been warned over the past 25 years about sexual misconduct or improper behaviour were still teaching in the state's schools.

"I am advised...that some of the 106 cases concern allegations related to inappropriate behaviour rather than sexual abuse or sexual assault," Carr said. "This is why these teachers are currently being monitored."
Such inappropriate behaviour included a teacher bumping into a female student in a crowded corridor and another teacher who had commented on a student's dress.
The more serious cases include a teacher who was dismissed and later reinstated on appeal after it was alleged he had intercourse with a student.
The prosecution against another teacher failed after it was alleged he had sexually assaulted a disabled child in 1992.
Carr said copies of child protection procedures would be given to each of the education department's 66,000 employees, all of whom would undergo child protection training.
